headline: Friday is the last very warm day before a cooling, dry weekend, and then a strengthening storm fed by a weak to moderate atmospheric river (a long plume of Pacific moisture) is increasingly likely to bring heavy rain, wind, possible thunderstorms and flash-flood risk Tuesday into Wednesday.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: High pressure overhead gives coastal and valley areas, including Carlsbad, one last very warm, dry day Friday under mostly clear skies. High clouds thicken Friday evening, which should keep low coastal clouds from becoming widespread overnight, though patchy low clouds are possible (about a 40 percent chance near San Diego and 25 percent near Santa Ana late tonight).

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Saturday brings more high clouds and cooling as the high pressure weakens, mainly in the western valleys, where highs drop into the 70s to near 80. Cooling spreads inland Sunday with stronger ocean breezes and breezier conditions in the mountains and deserts, where mountain highs stay in the 50s and 60s. Light showers become possible late Sunday night into Monday morning, but most areas from the coast to the coastal mountain slopes get about a quarter inch or less, and temperatures cool to within about 5 degrees of normal.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Heavier rain arrives late Monday night or Tuesday morning as a deepening storm pulls in a weak to locally moderate atmospheric river, sweeping northwest to southeast Tuesday and ending sometime Wednesday morning or afternoon. Early estimates are 1 inch or more and locally near 3 inches west of the mountains (highest in the LA basin), around half an inch in the lower deserts with some spots over an inch, and higher totals in the high desert; thunderstorms are more likely than usual, raising the risk of flash flooding, and strong winds are expected, most impactful near the coast though speeds are uncertain. Snow levels start above 8,000 feet Tuesday morning and fall to around 6,000 feet, bringing a chance of snow to the San Bernardino Mountain villages. After a brief dry break later Wednesday into early Thursday, a weak low pressure system may bring more cool, showery weather late next week.

coast: High tides keep dropping this weekend, to around 7 feet Saturday and below 7 feet Sunday, running about a foot above normal predictions; Saturday morning's high tide plus elevated surf brings minor to locally moderate coastal flooding. A long-period west swell produces 3 to 5 foot breakers with sets to 6 feet on exposed west-facing beaches Friday, building Saturday to 4 to 7 feet with sets to 8 feet on exposed west-facing beaches and near piers, highest in the morning and early afternoon, under a Beach Hazards Statement for the Orange and San Diego County coasts through Saturday afternoon. No hazardous boating conditions are expected through Monday, but southwest winds build Tuesday with widespread gusts of 30 to 35 knots (about 35 to 40 mph) Tuesday morning through Wednesday morning, steep, choppy high seas, and a 40 to 50 percent chance of storm-force gusts Tuesday morning and afternoon.
watch_for: Rain totals and thunderstorm/flash-flood risk with Tuesday–Wednesday's storm, which could still shift in track and strength
Strong winds Tuesday, especially near the coast
Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding and big surf Saturday morning
confidence: Forecasters are confident in the dry, cooling weekend and unusually confident this far out in the timing of the Tuesday–Wednesday storm, but rain totals, wind speeds and impacts are still uncertain, as is the pattern late next week.
